The usual measure is the **standardized difference** for each covariate — the difference in means between treated and control, divided by the pooled standard deviation so that age (in years) and a religion dummy (a proportion) sit on the same scale. A common rule of thumb treats anything under 0.1 in absolute value as balanced.

```{r balance}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "code"

# the confounders as columns of the design matrix: age plus a dummy for each category
Xmat <- model.matrix(~ age + sex + race + religion, data = ces)[, -1]
colnames(Xmat) <- str_remove(colnames(Xmat), "^(sex|race|religion)")

# standardized difference in means, treated minus control, with optional weights;
# the denominator is the unweighted pooled SD, so before and after share a scale
std_diff <- function(x, d, w) {
  sd_pool <- sqrt((var(x[d == 1]) + var(x[d == 0])) / 2)
  (weighted.mean(x[d == 1], w[d == 1]) - weighted.mean(x[d == 0], w[d == 0])) / sd_pool
}

balance <- map_dfr(colnames(Xmat), function(v) tibble(
  covariate          = v,
  `before weighting` = std_diff(Xmat[, v], ces$college, rep(1, nrow(ces))),
  `after weighting`  = std_diff(Xmat[, v], ces$college, ces$ipw))) %>%
  pivot_longer(-covariate, names_to = "sample", values_to = "std_diff") %>%
  mutate(covariate = fct_reorder(covariate, abs(std_diff), .fun = max),
         sample = factor(sample, levels = c("before weighting", "after weighting")))

max_before <- max(abs(balance$std_diff[balance$sample == "before weighting"]))
max_after  <- max(abs(balance$std_diff[balance$sample == "after weighting"]))
```

```{r}
#| include: false

alt_balance <- sprintf("Dot plot of standardized differences for 19 covariate categories. Before weighting (open grey circles) the differences range up to %.2f in absolute value: graduates are younger, more often Jewish, atheist, or male, and less often Black, Protestant, or 'nothing in particular'. After weighting (filled green dots) every difference sits at zero, the largest %.3f.", max_before, max_after)
```

```{r balance-fig}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "code"
#| label: fig-balance
#| fig-cap: "Standardized differences between graduates and non-graduates on each confounder, before and after inverse-probability weighting. The shaded band is ±0.1."
#| fig-alt: !expr alt_balance
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 6

ggplot(balance, aes(std_diff, covariate)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -0.1, xmax = 0.1, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = bu_greyfill, alpha = 0.52) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = bu_grey) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = sample, color = sample), size = 2.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(bu_grey, bu_green)) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(1, 16)) +
  labs(x = "standardized difference, college minus no college", y = NULL,
       color = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme_bu() +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

The open circles in @fig-balance are the confounding we worried about in the running example, now measured. Before weighting, graduates are younger, more often male, Jewish, or atheist, and less often Black, Protestant, or "nothing in particular"; the largest gap is `r round(max_before, 2)` standard deviations, for age. After weighting, every gap closes — the largest is `r sprintf("%.3f", max_after)`. The weights did their job: in the weighted sample, graduates and non-graduates have the same distribution of the confounders we measured, which is what a randomized experiment would have given us on those variables.

Read @fig-balance with the DAG in mind. The open circles are the $X \rightarrow D$ arrow at work — age, sex, race, and religion predicting who has a degree. The filled dots show that arrow cut: in the weighted sample, $X$ no longer predicts $D$. In omitted-variable-bias terms, weighting set $\delta_1$ to zero, so $\beta_2\delta_1$ is zero no matter how strongly $X$ affects the vote. The balance plot shows that weighting by propensity scores did what we had hoped.

Once again though, notice what the figure does not show. Family income and parental education are not on it, because we do not have them. Balance on the measured covariates says nothing about balance on the unmeasured ones, which is why a good balance plot is necessary but never sufficient in evaluating how effectively we've dealt with selection bias.

Matching on the propensity score itself is the other standard use of these scores; packages like `MatchIt` automate it. Like other propensity score approaches, matching derives from the same models (e.g. logit) we're accustomed to; matching also falls into the "selection on observables" approach.

# Two models, one estimand

Routes one and two landed on essentially the same number, but they got there differently. Route one worked on the $X \rightarrow Y$ arrow and needed the outcome model to be right. Route two worked on the $X \rightarrow D$ arrow and needed the treatment model to be right. Neither needed the other's model.

And notice something about *this* result: the two routes agreed. Two estimators built on two different models, landing on essentially the same number, is a reassurance — a rough specification check. Had they diverged sharply, that would be a red flag that one of the two models is misspecified, and worth chasing down before believing either.

## Which to use, and when

Because each route needs only its own model, the two fail in different places. A misspecified outcome model can wreck route one while route two is untouched, and a misspecified treatment model can wreck route two while route one is fine. That answers "which one?" directly: **work on the arrow you understand.**

- **If you understand how units came to be treated** — an admissions rule, a program assigned by a formula, a policy rolled out by known criteria — the $X \rightarrow D$ arrow is the one you can model well. Build the treatment model and weight: route two.
- **If you understand how the outcome is produced** better than how treatment was assigned, model the outcome and g-compute: route one. Route one also has practical advantages. As the ATE, ATT, and CATE subsections showed, it hands you any estimand you like just by choosing which units to average the predictions over, and it extends cleanly to treatments that are not a simple 0/1.
- **The two fail differently when overlap is poor.** Route two fails visibly: as @tbl-weights showed, a unit whose treatment is unusual for its profile gets a large weight, and a unit with a propensity score near 0 or 1 gets an enormous one, so the estimate lurches. Route one fails quietly: the outcome model extrapolates into covariate regions with no comparison units and returns a confident-looking prediction anyway. Either way, check overlap.
- **If you are not sure about either model, use both.** The doubly-robust estimator, next, combines them and needs only one of the two to be right.

## Using both: the doubly-robust estimator

**You do not actually have to choose.** There is an estimator that uses *both* models, and so works on both arrows at once — the **doubly-robust**, or **augmented inverse-probability-weighting** (AIPW), estimator [@bangrobins2005]. The idea is to start from the g-computation prediction and add an inverse-probability-weighted correction built from the model's residuals:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat\tau_{\text{DR}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \Bigg\{ & \left[ \hat m_1(X_i) + \frac{D_i\,\big(Y_i - \hat m_1(X_i)\big)}{\hat e(X_i)} \right] \\
& - \left[ \hat m_0(X_i) + \frac{(1 - D_i)\,\big(Y_i - \hat m_0(X_i)\big)}{1 - \hat e(X_i)} \right] \Bigg\},
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\hat m_1$ and $\hat m_0$ are the outcome-model predictions at $D = 1$ and $D = 0$ (the `p1` and `p0` from route one) and $\hat e$ is the propensity score (from route two). The property this buys is the one in the name: the estimator is **consistent if *either* the outcome model or the treatment model is correct** — you do not need both to be right. Read the formula with that in mind. If the outcome model is right, the residuals $Y_i - \hat m(X_i)$ average to zero, the correction terms vanish, and you are left with plain g-computation. If instead the outcome model is wrong but the *treatment* model is right, the inverse-probability weighting on those residuals is exactly what fixes up the biased predictions. Two chances to be right instead of one. We already have every piece, so we can build it by hand:

```{r aipw}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "code"

# Doubly-robust (AIPW) ATE: the g-computation predictions (p1, p0) PLUS an
# inverse-probability correction built from the outcome-model residuals and the
# propensity score. Consistent if EITHER the outcome model OR the treatment
# model is right -- not necessarily both.
aipw_ate <- with(ces,
  mean( (p1 + college       * (voteDem - p1) / pscore) -
        (p0 + (1 - college) * (voteDem - p0) / (1 - pscore)) ))
aipw_ate
```

That turns out to be about `r round(aipw_ate, 3)`, right alongside the other two — no surprise here, where both models are reasonable and already agree. The doubly-robust estimator is most useful when you are *unsure* about one of them: it is the default once you have built both a treatment model and an outcome model and would rather not stake the whole analysis on a single one being right.  

## All the estimates together

@fig-estimates puts the raw difference and the three estimators side by side. None of the three adjusted estimators comes with a simple analytic standard error once the propensity score is estimated, so I bootstrap all four the same way: resample respondents with replacement, refit both logits, recompute every estimate, and repeat 200 times. The intervals are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the 200 draws.

```{r bootstrap}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "code"

# all four estimates from one data set: refit both logits, then compute each
estimators <- function(dat) {
  ps <- glm(college ~ age + sex + race + religion, data = dat, family = binomial(link = "logit"))
  om <- glm(voteDem ~ college + age + sex + race + religion, data = dat, family = binomial(link = "logit"))
  e  <- predict(ps, type = "response")
  m1 <- predict(om, mutate(dat, college = 1), type = "response")
  m0 <- predict(om, mutate(dat, college = 0), type = "response")
  D  <- dat$college
  Y  <- dat$voteDem
  c(`raw difference`    = mean(Y[D == 1]) - mean(Y[D == 0]),
    `g-computation (route one)` = mean(m1 - m0),
    `IPW (route two)`   = mean(D * Y / e - (1 - D) * Y / (1 - e)),
    `doubly robust (AIPW)`      = mean((m1 + D * (Y - m1) / e) - (m0 + (1 - D) * (Y - m0) / (1 - e))))
}

point <- estimators(ces)

# 200 bootstrap resamples of respondents
boot_draws <- map_dfr(1:200, ~ estimators(slice_sample(ces, prop = 1, replace = TRUE)))

est_all <- tibble(estimator = names(point),
                  estimate  = point,
                  lo = map_dbl(boot_draws, quantile, 0.025),
                  hi = map_dbl(boot_draws, quantile, 0.975)) %>%
  mutate(estimator = fct_rev(fct_inorder(estimator)))
```

```{r}
#| include: false

alt_estimates <- sprintf("Four point estimates with 95 percent bootstrap intervals. The raw difference is %.3f. G-computation gives %.3f, IPW %.3f, and the doubly-robust estimator %.3f; their intervals overlap almost completely, and all three sit below the raw difference.", point[1], point[2], point[3], point[4])
```

```{r estimates-fig}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "code"
#| label: fig-estimates
#| fig-cap: "The raw difference and three estimates of the ATE of a college degree on Pr(Biden vote), with 95% bootstrap intervals (200 resamples)."
#| fig-alt: !expr alt_estimates
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.2

ggplot(est_all, aes(estimate, estimator)) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0.15, color = bu_green) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = bu_green) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.3f", estimate)), vjust = -1.1, size = 3.6, color = bu_black) +
  labs(x = "effect of a college degree on Pr(Biden vote)", y = NULL) +
  theme_bu() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

The three adjusted estimates land within a few thousandths of each other, and all three sit below the raw difference by about the size of the selection bias we computed above. Two different models, and a third that combines them, tell the same story. What none of them can tell us is whether family income and parental education would move all three together — the estimators agree because they share an assumption, and agreement is not evidence for the assumption.


# Where this sits: the landscape of causal identification

We have now built three estimators — g-computation, IPW, and the doubly-robust combination — and all three belong to the family we named at the start, selection on observables. They rest on the same assumption, conditional ignorability: the bet that the covariates we measured close every backdoor between treatment and outcome. This section sets that family beside the other one, design-based methods. We are not teaching those here, but you should be able to recognize them and know when you would need them, especially since you already know the architecture of some of them. Choosing between the two families is really choosing *what you are willing to assume*.

The one axis that organizes everything: **what defends the estimate against *unobserved* confounding?**

**Selection on observables** - nothing. These methods *assume* the confounding away, via ignorability, and then differ only in the mechanics of adjusting for the measured $X$:

- **Regression adjustment.** Put $X$ in the outcome model alongside $D$ and read off the average marginal effect of $D$. This is g-computation with a single model and no weighting — the plainest version of the idea, and the one you have been doing since the binary-models weeks.
- **Matching.** Pair each treated unit with control units that have a similar covariate profile (or a similar propensity score), discard the un-matchable, and difference the outcomes. Same ignorability assumption; the adjustment is done by *building comparable groups* rather than by modeling a functional form. This is the tool you will actually see most often in applied political science.
- **Propensity-score weighting (IPW).** Reweight units by the inverse of their propensity score so treated and control match on $X$, then compare — route two.
- **G-computation.** Model the outcome and average the predicted contrast — route one.
- **Doubly-robust (AIPW).** Combine the treatment and outcome models; right if either is.

All five are cousins. They condition on observables and hope that is enough. When it is not — when you cannot believe you measured the confounders — identification has to come from somewhere other than the covariates. That is the second family.

**Design-based methods** get their leverage from a *feature of how treatment was assigned*, and that feature can defend against unobserved confounding. You have seen the architecture of the first one already:

- **Instrumental variables (IV / 2SLS).** Find an instrument $Z$ that shifts the treatment $D$ but affects the outcome $Y$ *only* through $D$. That condition is the exclusion restriction. The instrument's as-good-as-random variation is transmitted to $D$, so the part of $D$ driven by $Z$ is unconfounded, even by unobservables. In DAG terms, the graph is $Z \rightarrow D \rightarrow Y$ with an unmeasured $U$ pointing into both $D$ and $Y$; the exclusion restriction is the claim that there is no arrow from $Z$ to $Y$, and no backdoor path into $Z$. The price is a narrower estimand: 2SLS recovers a **local** average treatment effect, the effect for the units whose treatment the instrument actually moved (the compliers), not the whole-population ATE.
- **Regression discontinuity (RD).** Treatment is assigned by a threshold on a running variable — a vote share above 50%, a test score above a cutoff. Units just below and just above the threshold are, on everything except treatment, essentially identical, so comparing them identifies an effect *local to the cutoff*. The design does the work; no ignorability-on-covariates is required.
- **Difference-in-differences (DiD).** With panel data, compare the before-to-after change in treated units to the same change in untreated units. Any confounder that is fixed over time differences out, so unobserved *time-invariant* confounding is handled by the design. The identifying assumption moves to **parallel trends**: absent treatment, the two groups would have moved in parallel.

Here is the same landscape as a table:

| Family | Methods | Identifying assumption | Handles *unobserved* confounding? | Typical estimand |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Selection on observables** (this week) | regression adjustment, matching, IPW, g-computation, doubly-robust | conditional ignorability — measured $X$ closes every backdoor | **No** — assumed away | ATE, ATT, CATE |
| **Design-based** (a second course) | IV / 2SLS, RD, difference-in-differences | a design feature: an instrument, a threshold, parallel trends | **Yes** — that is the point | often local (LATE, effect at the cutoff, effect on treated periods) |

So, **when would we use the tools from this week?** When selection on observables is credible — when we have good substantive reason to believe the confounders are measured and in the model. That is a strong condition, and often it is not met; family income and parental education really are missing from our CES data, and @fig-dag-ces shows the paths they leave open. But sometimes it is met; for two political-science examples, see @gilligansergenti2008 and @blattman2009. When you cannot defend ignorability, the honest move is not a fancier weighting scheme — it is to go find a design: an instrument, a discontinuity, a policy change with a clean before-and-after. The methods in this week and the methods in that second course are not really competitors; they are answers to a different question about the data you have: *did I measure the confounders, or do I need a design to handle the ones I did not?*

# Selection and censoring as causal missingness

Return to the switching equation. A causal effect was a missing-data problem — the untreated outcome of a treated unit is missing by construction. **Selection** and **censoring** are the same problem wearing different clothes:

- **Sample selection** (Heckman): we observe $Y_i$ only for units that cleared some selection hurdle, and the hurdle is related to $Y$. The unobserved outcomes are missing *not* at random.
- **Censoring** (durations, Week 11): we observe that an event had not happened by the end of observation, but not when it eventually would — the survival time is missing, informatively.

Our running example is itself a selected sample. We only see a vote for respondents who turned out, turnout is affected by the treatment, and in @fig-dag-ces that made turnout a collider we conditioned on by building the sample. The Biden-vote outcome of a graduate who stayed home is missing, and so is the one of a non-graduate who stayed home — and whether they are missing depends on college and, plausibly, on family income. That is the same missing-data problem as the switching equation, one step earlier.

The collider algebra from the DAG section applies here too. Restricting the sample to voters is conditioning on turnout by selection rather than by putting it in the model. Among the selected, the average of the outcome equation's error, $E[\varepsilon_i \mid D_i, \text{selected}]$, depends on $D_i$ whenever something that drives selection also drives the outcome. That is the same leak of the outcome's error into the conditioning variable that produced the $\lambda$ term above. Heckman's correction adds a term to the outcome equation, the inverse Mills ratio, that models exactly that conditional mean. Put in DAG terms, a Heckman selection model is a repair for having conditioned on a collider.

We are not building a Heckman selection model as a standalone topic this term. The point here is the *conceptual* one: whenever the data we would need to identify an effect are systematically absent, we are back in the potential-outcomes frame, reasoning about what is missing and whether we can defend an assumption that lets us fill it in. That reasoning recurs — in the count models (effects on rates) and the duration models (effects on hazards, and censoring head-on).


# Take-away points

**The problem**

1. A causal effect is defined by potential outcomes, and it is fundamentally a missing-data problem: we never see both $Y_i(1)$ and $Y_i(0)$. We cannot estimate individual effects, but we can target averages — the ATE, ATT, and CATE.
2. The raw difference between treated and untreated equals the ATT plus selection bias. In the running example, a raw difference of about 0.16 is an effect of about 0.13 plus selection bias of about 0.03.

**The assumption**

3. Identification needs assumptions the data cannot supply: conditional ignorability and positivity.
4. A DAG makes the ignorability assumption visible and tells us what to condition on. Condition on confounders to close backdoor paths; leave mediators alone if you want the total effect; never condition on a collider. Do not condition on anything the treatment affects — and remember that selecting the sample is a way of conditioning.
5. The adjustment set changes the answer: about 0.16 with no adjustment, 0.13 adjusting for the confounders, 0.04 adding party ID, a mediator. In omitted-variable-bias terms, the first of these removes bias and the second removes part of the total effect. The regression cannot tell the two apart — only the direction of the arrows can.

**Two ways to remove the bias**

6. Selection bias travels along the backdoor path $D \leftarrow X \rightarrow Y$, which needs both arrows. Remove either one and the bias is gone: the omitted-variable bias $\beta_2\delta_1$ is zero if either $\beta_2$ or $\delta_1$ is.
7. Route one, g-computation, deals with the $X \rightarrow Y$ arrow using the outcome model. It is the average marginal effect from the quantities-of-interest week, reinterpreted as an ATE under ignorability. Average its unit-level contrasts over everyone for the ATE, over the treated for the ATT, over a group for a CATE. In a logit those contrasts vary through compression alone; if you want the data to decide whether the effect differs by group, add the product term.
8. Route two, the propensity score, cuts the $X \rightarrow D$ arrow using the treatment model — a logit pointed at the treatment. Weighting on it balances the measured covariates, and the balance plot checks that the arrow is cut. It cannot certify ignorability, because it says nothing about what we did not measure.
9. Work on the arrow you understand. If you are unsure about both, the doubly-robust (AIPW) estimator uses both models and is consistent if *either* is right.

**The limits**

10. These are all **selection-on-observables** methods: they assume unobserved confounding away. When you cannot defend that assumption, you need a design — IV, RD, difference-in-differences — that gets identification from the assignment mechanism instead.
11. Selection and censoring are causal missingness — the same frame, returning later in the term.
